CHIEF COMPLAINT
Second opinion regarding right index finger

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Philip Gutierrez is a 50-year-old right-handed male presenting for a second opinion regarding his right index finger. He sustained a hyperextension injury to his right index finger during a motor vehicle accident in March 2026 when he was a passenger in a vehicle that was rear-ended multiple times, which slung him forward and caused extension of his right index finger. He has had persistent pain and swelling since the injury, which he describes as sometimes unbearable and interfering with his ability to drive and work as an X-ray technician. He reports inability to make a fist. He was previously evaluated by an orthopedist and referred to occupational therapy. An MRI was obtained showing a partial-thickness tear of the flexor digitorum superficialis tendon. He was initially offered a steroid injection but declined due to concerns about steroid side effects, specifically noting a prior reaction to dexamethasone causing tachycardia and a reaction to methylprednisolone causing itching. Current radiographs show no bony abnormalities or arthritis.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies diabetes mellitus. Denies rheumatoid arthritis.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Adverse reaction to dexamethasone (tachycardia)
Adverse reaction to methylprednisolone (itching)

MEDICATIONS
Blood pressure medication

ALLERGIES
Dexamethasone - causes tachycardia
Methylprednisolone - causes itching

FAMILY HISTORY
Not discussed.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Occupation: X-ray technician
Dominant hand: Right
Motor vehicle accident: Passenger

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Pleasant, cooperative, healthy male in no distress
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, 2+ radial pulses
Right hand: No swelling or bruising in the palm. Normal volar surface creases with slightly diminished skin creases over the PIP joint compared to the middle finger. Index finger rests in 10-degree PIP-flexed position. Tenderness with passive correction of PIP position. Mild paresthesias present. Flexor digitorum profundus intact with ability to flex distal interphalangeal joint. Flexor digitorum superficialis with partial tear and limited function. Extensor tendons intact. Radial and ulnar collateral ligaments intact. Pain with active and passive range of motion attempts.

RESULTS
Right hand radiographs (4 views today): No bony abnormalities, joint congruency throughout all lesser digits, no soft tissue shadows of concern, no arthritis.

MRI (dated 4/24/2021 in records): Focal soft tissue swelling over right index metacarpophalangeal joint, partial-thickness tear of right flexor digitorum superficialis tendon, fluid consistent with tenosynovitis around flexor digitorum profundus and flexor digitorum superficialis tendons, radial and ulnar collateral ligaments of index metacarpophalangeal joint intact, metacarpophalangeal joint capsule intact, extensor tendons intact.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Post-traumatic severe stenosing tenosynovitis of right index finger with partial-thickness tear of flexor digitorum superficialis tendon. Significant scar tissue and post-traumatic inflammation around the flexor digitorum superficialis tendon blocking excursion of other tendons. Flexor digitorum profundus remains intact.

1. Steroid injection: Attempted betamethasone (Celestone) 1 cc with lidocaine 0.5 cc. During first attempt, patient experienced dramatic and violent painful reaction to needle introduction with hand contortion and withdrawal prompting cessation. Second injection attempt made with same agents. Small palmar vein bled scantly, cleaned and band-aid applied. Patient reassured on multiple occasions that no harm was done to finger.
2. Avoid dexamethasone-based injections.
3. Ice this evening.
4. Ibuprofen as needed.
5. Outpatient occupational or physical therapy once weekly for 6 weeks with goal of full active and passive range of motion with no restrictions.
6. Patient counseled on importance of active movement and that splinting immobilizes rather than mobilizes. Reassured that finger is safe to move as extensors and collateral ligaments are intact.
7. Possible repeat steroid injection if needed.
8. Safe to drive.
